title: Deliberate practice
keyIdea: Deliberate practice is practice designed to improve one specific weakness. You work just beyond what you can already do, in the stretch zone where you get things right most of the time but not always. You get fast feedback on every try, give it your full attention, and repeat until the weak spot is fixed. Hours spent replaying what you can already do level off, however many there are.

kid: Two people can practise for the same hours and end up at very different levels. One plays through what she already knows. It feels good, but she stops getting better. The other finds his weakest spot and works on that. He keeps improving.

Deliberate practice has four parts. First, pick one weak spot, such as a tricky bar of music or one type of maths question. Second, work in the stretch zone. That means hard enough that you make some mistakes, but not so hard that you are lost. Third, get feedback on every try, straight away. Fourth, give it your full attention.

Feedback is the key. If you cannot see what went wrong, you cannot fix it. You might keep making the same mistake for weeks. A coach, a mark scheme, or a recording of yourself can show you each mistake while it is fresh.
This kind of practice is hard work and not always fun. So keep sessions short, and stop when your focus slips. Twenty focused minutes on a weak spot often beats two hours of easy repetition.
adult: The term comes from Anders Ericsson's research on expert performance. In his 1993 study of violinists, the best players had spent more hours on solitary practice built to fix specific weaknesses. Simply playing more did not explain the gap. He later stressed that naive practice, repeating what you can already do, tends to plateau once a skill becomes automatic.

A common mistake is the 10,000-hour rule, which Ericsson himself said was a misreading of his work. Hours matter only when they are focused and hard. Be careful in the other direction too: a 2014 meta-analysis by Macnamara and colleagues found deliberate practice explained about a quarter of the differences in games, a fifth in music, and much less in education and jobs. Starting age, teaching and other factors also count.

For a 16 or 17 year old, this links to metacognition and self-regulated learning, as in the EEF guidance. Students plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning. In practice: use mock results to find the weakest topic, set questions at a level where you get about 60 to 85 percent right, mark each answer straight away, and fix one thing at a time.

The lab shows each idea in a toy model. Two players practise the same hours with different results. A piece sounds only as good as its weakest bar. A difficulty dial shows learning peak in the stretch zone. In an aiming drill, the drift can only be fixed once feedback appears. Last, the learner sorts real study plans.

familyTip: Before your next revision session, look at your last test or mock and name the one topic that lost you the most marks. Spend 20 minutes on just that topic with questions you can mark straight away, then note what you got wrong and why.

visual.caption: Deliberate practice or just repetition? Drag each plan, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Loop the hardest four bars slowly, then speed up
Play the whole song you already know, again
Past questions on your weakest topic, marked after each one
Thirty easy questions you always get right
Film your serve and fix one thing a coach points out
Revise for three hours with your phone buzzing
Redraft one paragraph using your teacher's comment
Re-read your notes until they feel familiar

lab.caption: Flagship lab: same hours with different results, fix the weakest bar, find the stretch zone, and correct your aim with feedback.

practice.prompt: Sam has played chess online every day for two years but stopped improving. What would help most?
choices: Study his lost games and drill the positions he gets wrong
Play even more quick games
Accept he has reached his limit
practice.hint: Which choice targets a specific weakness with feedback?
practice.explain: More of the same levels off. Studying his losses finds the weak spot and gives feedback, so he can practise exactly what goes wrong.

practice.prompt: In a practice set you get {a} out of 20 right. What percentage is that?
practice.hint: Each question out of 20 is worth 5%.
practice.explain: {a} out of 20 is {=a*5}%. That is right most of the time but not always, so the set is in the stretch zone.

practice.prompt: A piece has five bars. Four play cleanly 90% of the time and one only {a}% of the time. In the lab model, the whole piece is as good as its weakest bar. What percentage is that?
practice.hint: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Which bar is lowest?
practice.explain: The weakest bar plays cleanly {a}% of the time, so the whole piece does too. That bar is where practice should go.

practice.prompt: Which shows deliberate practice for a weak backhand in tennis?
choices: 100 backhands at a target, coach calling each one
A friendly match mostly using forehands
Hitting while chatting with friends
practice.hint: Look for one weakness, feedback and full attention.
practice.explain: Repeated backhands at a target, with a coach's call after each one, target the weakness with fast feedback and full focus.

pool.prompt: Out of 20 tries at a new skill, you get {a} right. Which zone are you in?
choices: Stretch zone
Comfort zone
Panic zone
pool.hint: Work out the percentage, then compare it with 60 to 85%.
pool.explain: {a} out of 20 is {=a*5}%: right most of the time but not always, so this is the stretch zone.

pool.prompt: You get {a} of 20 right at level 3 and {b} of 20 right at level 6. Which level is in the stretch zone (60 to 85% right)?
pool.hint: Turn each score into a percentage. Each question is 5%.
pool.explain: Level 3 gives {=a*5}%, which is too easy. Level 6 gives {=b*5}%, in the stretch zone, so practise at level 6.

pool.prompt: What is the main thing that makes practice deliberate?
choices: It targets a specific weakness, with feedback
It lasts for many hours
It feels easy and relaxing
pool.hint: Ana and Ben had the same hours.
pool.explain: Deliberate practice aims at one weakness, just beyond your current level, with feedback on each try. Hours alone do not make it deliberate.

choices: You can correct the next try while this one is fresh
It makes sessions longer
It does not matter
pool.hint: Think of the blind shots in the aiming drill.
pool.explain: Without feedback the drift in the aiming drill stayed hidden. Fast feedback shows each error, so the next try can be corrected.

pool.prompt: Priya's essay comes back with eight comments. What is the best deliberate-practice plan?
choices: Choose one, like topic sentences, and redraft for that
Fix all eight at once in a full rewrite
Write a new essay and hope
pool.hint: Full attention on one thing at a time.
pool.explain: Working on one weakness at a time keeps attention focused and makes the feedback clear. Trying to fix everything at once splits attention.

pool.prompt: A friend says anyone becomes an expert after 10,000 hours. What is the best reply?
choices: Hours help only if they are focused and hard
Yes, hours are all that matter
No, practice never helps
pool.hint: Ericsson said the 10,000-hour rule misread his work.
pool.explain: Ericsson found that the kind of practice mattered, not just the hours. Replaying easy material levels off however long you do it.

pool.prompt: You always score 100% on your revision quizzes. What should you change?
choices: Make them harder until you make some mistakes
Nothing, it is working
Switch to the hardest paper you can find
pool.explain: Always 100% is the comfort zone, with nothing left to fix. Raise the level until you get most, but not all, right.

pool.prompt: Which session is most likely to be deliberate practice?
choices: 20 focused minutes on your weakest topic, marking each answer
Two hours re-reading notes
An hour of questions with music videos on
pool.hint: Look for a weak spot, feedback and full attention.
pool.explain: Twenty focused minutes on the weakest topic, with each answer marked, has all the parts. Re-reading and split attention do not.
